newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China says HK emigrants have grace period to return.
newsitem.headline: China says HK emigrants have grace period to return.

text.p: China, tackling an issue worrying Hong Kong emigrants around the world, on Friday gave them a grace period to return to the territory if they want to keep permanent residency rights.
Wang Fengchao, deputy director of Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, told a seminar on the Hong Kong transition that emigrants could keep their right of abode if they want to.
China is taking Hong Kong back from Britain on July 1 after a century and a half of colonial rule in the territory.
An estimated 750,000 of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people have foreign citizenship. The bulk have made Canada, Australia, Britain or the United States their adopted homes.
Under the post-1997 constitution called the Basic Law, residents with foreign passports can retain right of abode, but if they are abroad for long after July 1 they might lose it.
However, Wang said China was prepared to allow them a grace period, but the length of time would be set by the post-handover government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR).
"As to the length of time they are allowed to stay outside Hong Kong, this is for the SAR to decide," he said.
Tam Yiu-chung, a member of the future cabinet of Hong Kong Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa, said he believed the period would be up to three years.
Tam said he was confident of being able to draft by July 1 laws to resolve the right of abode issue, which has bogged down Sino-British negotiations on handover details.
Wong Siu-yin, an emigrants' group representative, welcomed Wang's comments.
"I think this is very good and very loose. I think they will welcome those Hong Kong people who have emigrated to return to Hong Kong to live," Wong told reporters.
Beijing's Wang said emigrants would be able to retain right of abode as long as they did not declare a foreign nationality.
Even emigrants who had lost their Hong Kong right of abode could live and work in Hong Kong without restrictions, he said.

Returnees who do not declare their overseas nationalities when they come back are regarded as Chinese nationals and can have the right of abode, but many are anxious about how China might treat them if they forfeit foreign consular protection in favour of Hong Kong right of abode.

Wang said returnees would be treated as leniently as possible. "Even for those who have lost the right of abode, we will still allow them to enter and leave Hong Kong freely and they will not be bound by restrictions set out in residence regulations and will be able to live and work in Hong Kong."
